entries.name: Monitor
entries.description:
Start a background monitor that streams events from a long-running script. Each stdout line is an event — you keep working and notifications arrive in the chat. Events arrive on their own schedule and are not replies from the user, even if one lands while you're waiting for the user to answer a question.

Pick by how many notifications you need:
- **One** ("tell me when the server is ready / the build finishes") → use **Bash with `run_in_background`** and a command that exits when the condition is true, e.g. `until grep -q "Ready in" dev.log; do sleep 0.5; done`. You get a single completion notification when it exits.
- **One per occurrence, until the monitor expires (re-arm to continue)** ("tell me every time an ERROR line appears") → Monitor with an unbounded command (`tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, `while true`).
- **One per occurrence, until a known end** ("emit each CI step result, stop when the run completes") → Monitor with a command that emits lines and then exits.

Your script's stdout is the event stream. Each line becomes a notification. Exit ends the watch.

  # Each matching log line is an event
  tail -f /var/log/app.log | grep --line-buffered "ERROR"

  # Each file change is an event
  inotifywait -m --format '%e %f' /watched/dir

  # Poll GitHub for new PR comments and emit one line per new comment
  last=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
  while true; do
    now=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
    gh api "repos/owner/repo/issues/123/comments?since=$last" --jq '.[] | "\(.user.login): \(.body)"'
    last=$now; sleep 30
  done

  # Node script that emits events as they arrive (e.g. WebSocket listener)
  node watch-for-events.js

  # Per-occurrence with a natural end: emit each CI check as it lands, exit when the run completes
  prev=""
  while true; do
    s=$(gh pr checks 123 --json name,bucket)
    cur=$(jq -r '.[] | select(.bucket!="pending") | "\(.name): \(.bucket)"' <<<"$s" | sort)
    comm -13 <(echo "$prev") <(echo "$cur")
    prev=$cur
    jq -e 'all(.bucket!="pending")' <<<"$s" >/dev/null && break
    sleep 30
  done

**Don't use an unbounded command for a single notification.** `tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, and `while true` never exit on their own, so the monitor stays armed until timeout even after the event has fired. For "tell me when X is ready," use Bash `run_in_background` with an `until` loop instead (one notification, ends in seconds). Note that `tail -f log | grep -m 1 ...` does *not* fix this: if the log goes quiet after the match, `tail` never receives SIGPIPE and the pipeline hangs anyway.

**Script quality:**
- Every pipe stage must flush per line or matches sit in its buffer unseen: `grep` needs `--line-buffered`, `awk` needs `fflush()`. `head` cannot flush at all — `| head -N` delivers nothing until N matches accumulate, then ends the stream.
- In poll loops, handle transient failures (`curl ... || true`) — one failed request shouldn't kill the monitor.
- Poll intervals: 30s+ for remote APIs (rate limits), 0.5-1s for local checks.
- Write a specific `description` — it appears in every notification ("errors in deploy.log" not "watching logs").
- Only stdout is the event stream. Stderr goes to the output file (readable via Read) but does not trigger notifications — for a command you run directly (e.g. `python train.py 2>&1 | grep --line-buffered ...`), merge stderr with `2>&1` so its failures reach your filter. (No effect on `tail -f` of an existing log — that file only contains what its writer redirected.)

**Coverage — silence is not success.** When watching a job or process for an outcome, your filter must match every terminal state, not just the happy path. A monitor that greps only for the success marker stays silent through a crashloop, a hung process, or an unexpected exit — and silence looks identical to "still running." Before arming, ask: *if this process crashed right now, would my filter emit anything?* If not, widen it.

  # Wrong — silent on crash, hang, or any non-success exit
  tail -f run.log | grep --line-buffered "elapsed_steps="

  # Right — one alternation covering progress + the failure signatures you'd act on
  tail -f run.log | grep -E --line-buffered "elapsed_steps=|Traceback|Error|FAILED|assert|Killed|OOM"

For poll loops checking job state, emit on every terminal status (`succeeded|failed|cancelled|timeout`), not just success. If you cannot confidently enumerate the failure signatures, broaden the grep alternation rather than narrow it — some extra noise is better than missing a crashloop.

**Output volume**: Every stdout line is a conversation message, so the filter should be selective — but selective means "the lines you'd act on," not "only good news." Never pipe raw logs; filter to exactly the success and failure signals you care about. Monitors that produce too many events are automatically stopped; restart with a tighter filter if this happens.

Stdout lines within 200ms are batched into a single notification, so multiline output from a single event groups naturally.

The script runs in the same shell environment as Bash. Exit ends the watch (exit code is reported). Every monitor expires after `timeout_ms` (default 5 minutes, at most 30 minutes): it is killed and you get one notice with the event count. Re-arm it if you still need the watch; for a long watch (PR monitoring, log tails) set `timeout_ms` to the maximum and re-arm on each expiry, and widen the filter if an expiry with no events was unexpected. Use TaskStop to cancel early.
**ws source** — open a WebSocket and stream each incoming text frame as an event. No shell, no polling: the server pushes, you get notified.

  Monitor({
    ws: {url: 'wss://events.example.com/stream', protocols: ['v1']},
    description: 'deploy events',
  })

Each text frame becomes one notification (multiline frames stay as one event). Binary frames are reported as `[binary frame, N bytes]` rather than passed through. Socket close ends the watch with the close code surfaced; errors are surfaced before close. Same rate limiting as bash — a firehose will be suppressed and eventually stopped, so subscribe to a filtered feed where one exists.

Prefer this over `command: 'websocat wss://…'` — it avoids the extra process and line-buffering pitfalls. Use bash when you need to transform or filter frames with shell tools before they become events.

When an event lands that the user would want to act on now — an error appeared, the status they were waiting on flipped — send a PushNotification. Not every event is worth a push; the ones that change what they'd do next are.

command.description: Shell command or script. Each stdout line is an event; exit ends the watch.

ws.description: WebSocket to open. Each text frame is an event; binary frames are reported as a placeholder line. Socket close ends the watch. Cannot be combined with command.

fix(trailers): read the final block with git's comment prefix and separators

prepare-commit-msg assumed git strips "#" lines from an editor message.
With core.commentChar or core.commentString set to anything else, or
"auto" picking another prefix, git kept Entire's "# Remove the
Entire-Checkpoint trailer above" explanation, so the recorded commit
ended without a trailer block and post-commit condensed nothing. An
amend could not see the commit's own trailer behind git's comment block
and appended a second copy.

- Resolve git's comment prefix for editor sources (core.commentChar or
  core.commentString, aliases where the last one set wins; for "auto",
  read back from the comment block git wrote) and use it to strip the
  message, write the explanation, and place inherited trailers. A -m/-F
  message skips the lookup.
- Cut an editor message only at git's exact scissors line, so prose that
  mentions the marker neither hides a final trailer nor exposes a body
  one.
- Accept "Key:value" and tab separators in trailer lines, as git does,
  in both the final-block reader and the writer.

content.text:
I committed the three fixes locally as `866efab31`, on top of the PR head. The branch is 1 commit ahead of origin and merges cleanly with current main (`f36367e6f`). Nothing has been pushed or posted.

## What changed

- **Comment character:** prepare-commit-msg now uses git's real comment prefix: `core.commentChar` or `core.commentString` (the last one set wins), `#` when unset, and for `auto` it reads back the character git used in its own comment block. It's used when finding the commit's trailer, when writing Entire's explanation lines, and when placing inherited trailers. `-m`/`-F` commits skip the lookup.
- **Scissors line:** an editor message is cut only at git's exact scissors line, so a prose line that mentions the marker is kept.
- **Separators:** trailer lines accept `Key:value` and a tab after the colon, as git does. The reader and the writer still share one grammar.
- **Docs:** I updated the paragraph in `docs/architecture/sessions-and-checkpoints.md`.

## Verification

- **Tests failed first, for the expected reasons.**
  - 5 new integration tests running the real hook binary: editor commit and amend with `;` and with `auto`, plus the prose scissors case.
  - The attach no-space test.
  - 7 separator subtests.
  - The new-API unit tests couldn't compile before the change. So after the fix I put the old behaviors back one at a time in scratch copies (repo untouched), and each of the 6 was caught.
- **Real `git commit`**, with git writing the message and doing its own cleanup: all 6 cases pass (default, `;`, `//`, `auto` with a `#` template, amend with `;`, amend with `auto`).
- **Lint:** `mise run fmt && mise run lint` gives 0 issues.
- **Full suite** (`go test -tags=integration -race ./...`): 89 packages ok, including every trailer-authority and adversarial integration test. The failures are all outside this change:
  - hook-chain install, external-agent discovery and external-command signal tests timed out under race-mode load; all pass in isolation;
  - two Antigravity e2e tests fail on the unchanged head too, because they pick up your 1Password commit signing.
- **Canary:** Vogon 53/53, Roger-Roger 4/4.
- **Cost:** about 5.4 ms (median) for one `git config` call, only on editor-source commits. That's about the same as one `git rev-parse`.

**Follow-up, not in this commit:** the commit-msg hook's empty-message check still assumes `#`. Reading the code (I haven't run it): with `;`, quitting the editor without typing still produces a commit instead of aborting. Before this commit that commit held Entire's `#` helper text; now it holds just the trailer. It's about 5 lines plus a test, and could go in before pushing.

## Drafts for your approval

**Reply on [the scissors thread](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/2253#discussion_r4313606824):**

> agreed. git only cuts at a line that is exactly `<comment char> ------------------------ >8 ------------------------`, so a prose line containing the marker stays in the commit. i reproduced both orderings: a body trailer above such a line looks final after stripping, and a real final trailer below it disappears. fixed in 866efab31: `StripEditorComments` now cuts only at the exact scissors line for the configured comment character. added tests for both orderings and a CRLF line.

**Reply on [the separator thread](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/2253#discussion_r4313606970):**

> agreed. `git interpret-trailers --parse` reads `Entire-Checkpoint:<id>` and a tab separator as trailers, and main's `RemoveCheckpointTrailers` tests already treat both as trailer lines. fixed in 866efab31: `trailerLineRe` is now `^[A-Za-z][A-Za-z0-9-]*:`, shared by the reader and the writer so they still agree. leading whitespace is still rejected. added reader cases and an attach test that joins a no-space trailer.

**PR description edits:**

1. In **Fix**, replace the paragraph starting "Prepare reads the message as git will record it" with:
   > Prepare reads the message as git will record it (`trailers.StripEditorComments`): an editor message loses the lines starting with git's comment prefix and everything from the exact scissors line down, while a `-m`/`-F` message keeps every line as content. The prefix is `core.commentChar` or `core.commentString` (aliases, last one set wins), `#` when unset, and for `auto` it is read back from the comment block git wrote. Prepare writes its explanation and inherited trailers with the same prefix, so git's cleanup removes the explanation. Trailer lines accept `Key:value` and tab separators, as git does. The final-block reader rejects leading-whitespace pseudo-trailers, accepts indented lines only as continuations, and never reads the subject paragraph as trailers. The writer from #2259 uses the same `isTrailerBlock` grammar, so a trailer it appends is always one the readers accept.
2. In **Rejected alternatives**, replace the `core.commentChar` bullet with:
   > - Guessing `auto` from the whole message: once git has written its comment block, the character it chose always looks used, so the guess is wrong. The prefix is read back from git's own block instead.
3. In **Tests, verified RED before the fix**, add:
   > - `TestTrailerAuthority_EditorCommitHonorsCommentChar` and `TestTrailerAuthority_AmendHonorsCommentChar` (`;` and `auto`) failed: the recorded commit kept Entire's explanation and ended without a trailer block, and the amend appended a second trailer. `TestTrailerAuthority_ProseScissorsMarkerIsNotACut` failed with `prepare-commit-msg must stamp a trailer in the final block`, and `TestAttach_NoSpaceTrailerJoinsCheckpoint` with `attach wrote the session into <new id>, want the trailer's checkpoint a1b2c3d4e5f6`.
4. In **Test plan**, replace the test lines with:

   > - [x] `go test -tags=integration -race ./...`: 89 packages ok; the only failures are tests that pass in isolation (hook-chain install, external agent discovery, external-command signals under load) or fail on the unchanged head too (Antigravity e2e picking up a local commit-signing config)

content.thinking:
I'm considering how commit-msg hooks behave with -m commits specifically, since those messages lack the usual comment block and git's default cleanup mode treats '#' lines differently than during an interactive edit.

So if a user runs something like `git commit -m "#42 fix login"`, hasUserContent would treat that subject line as a comment since it starts with '#', skip it, and find no real content besides the appended checkpoint trailer — causing the trailer to get stripped and the checkpoint link to be lost. This looks like a genuine pre-existing bug affecting teams who prefix commit subjects with issue numbers like "#123: fix bug", and it exists in the current main branch code too, not just the new changes.

But then I realize the commit-msg hook can't actually distinguish whether the message came from an editor or from -m, since git only passes it the message file, not the source. The hook's purpose is specifically to preserve git's empty-message abort behavior for the editor flow — when someone opens an editor with the trailer pre-inserted and quits without adding anything, stripping the trailer back down to nothing lets git correctly abort. I need to figure out whether -m with an empty string triggers git's own abort before or after the hook runs.

The -m case breaks things: "-m '#42 fix login'" keeps the whole line as real content since git doesn't treat it as a comment there, so stripping the trailer based on the prefix rule alone would be wrong. To fix this properly I'd need to know the actual source of the message — either by having prepare-commit-msg stash that info in a marker file for commit-msg to read, by detecting git's comment-block instructional text (fragile across locales), or by narrowing the heuristic some other way.

A structural heuristic seems promising: treat comment-prefix lines as actual git comments only if the message's trailing block of lines starts with that prefix, meaning git's instructional block is still present. For the -m case, the trailer is the last line, not a comment block, so the '#42' line counts as real content and the trailer stays intact — correct behavior. For editor flow where the user leaves git's comment block in place, the last lines would match the prefix and still get stripped as expected.

Cases where the user's own -m message already includes a trailer-like line, or uses -e for editing, still resolve correctly under this heuristic. But I'm second-guessing scope: the -m '#42' edge case is really a separate pre-existing bug unrelated to comment-char handling, and I need to decide whether folding it into this same fix is justified by the governing rule or whether it deserves its own treatment.

I'm weighing two options: (A) minimal fix using just the comment prefix, which leaves the -m '#…' bug unresolved, versus (B) a trailing-block heuristic that also fixes it. I should verify the -m '#42' bug behavior against real git before deciding how to present this choice.

Checking the trailer-skip logic, I notice the "Entire-Checkpoint:" prefix check with TrimSpace will also catch indented or body trailer lines, which affects how CommitMsg determines if a message has a trailer versus just user content — this edge case seems acceptable though.

Now I'm working through gitCommentPrefix's "auto" behavior in commit-msg: after editing, git's comment block usually persists at the message's end unless deleted, and even in that deleted case the fallback logic (scanning for a leading punctuation character on the last line) should still find something usable like ';'. I'm also weighing the cost of calling gitCommentPrefix via subprocess for every linked commit — it's only invoked when a trailer is actually found, so I'm considering whether that call can be skipped in the common case since its only purpose is deciding hasUserContent.

For the hot path of agent commits using -m, I want to avoid the subprocess entirely by restructuring hasUserContent: if there's no trailing comment block, treat every non-blank, non-trailer line as user content; otherwise skip lines matching the prefix. The trick is figuring out how to detect "no trailing block" cheaply before needing the prefix at all.

If the last non-blank line is the trailer itself, content exists already so no prefix resolution is needed—that only matters when the message ends with git's leftover comment block instead, meaning I need to check if the user deleted all the comments and left just the trailer with nothing else, which would count as empty content.

Writing the strip logic...

I'm realizing the harder case: with `-m` and `-s`, git appends a Signed-off-by trailer before prepare-commit-msg even runs, so the last line might not be the Entire-Checkpoint trailer even though no comment block was ever added. I need to detect "editor-style" messages more reliably than just checking the last line.

I'm weighing whether the pre-check is actually safe, since commentChar could theoretically be a letter rather than the typical non-alphanumeric symbols, making this edge case rare but not impossible. I'm also questioning whether the extra few milliseconds in the commit-msg hook actually matters given the existing subprocess overhead, since the real performance concern raised previously was about the post-commit hook rather than this one.

Actually, I'm now spotting a bug with the -v flag: with a verbose commit, the last non-blank line of the message would be a diff line rather than something starting with the comment prefix, so my "last non-blank line starts with prefix" heuristic would wrongly conclude there's no comment block, causing the comment lines to be treated as real content and the empty-message detection to fail entirely.

So I need to handle the scissors line separately for -v: cut everything at the scissors line first (using the resolved comment prefix), then apply my last-line check to what remains before the cut. That still requires knowing the prefix via subprocess, so there's no avoiding that call. The flow becomes: resolve the prefix, cut at the scissors line, check if the last non-blank line before the cut starts with the prefix, and if so strip the comment block and check the remainder for real content — otherwise treat everything as user content for -m/-F cases.

Edge cases worry me though: `-F file` with trailing `#` comment lines but no editor invoked — git's cleanup still strips these in some modes, but my rule might misjudge whether there's real content if the file is entirely comment lines, causing a silent loss of the trailer instead of an abort. Also `--cleanup=verbatim` or `whitespace` modes keep comment lines in the final commit even though my logic would strip them when deciding if there's content, meaning I could wrongly conclude there's no user content and drop the trailer while git still commits the comment block as-is.

So I'm weighing two fixes: a minimal one that just swaps the hard-coded '#' for the actual configured comment prefix (plus scissors handling), versus a broader one that also fixes the pre-existing bug where `-m "#42 fix login"` silently drops the link because it's misread as a comment line. I should actually verify that `-m` bug against real git behavior before asserting it, using the scratch real-git overlay test setup.

I want to test several scenarios with hooks installed (prepare-commit-msg, commit-msg, post-commit): an empty message via ';' editor should abort the commit entirely, same with default '#' editor, `-m "#42 fix login"` should ideally keep the trailer but currently probably strips it, and a -v editor with empty input should also abort as a sanity check on scissors handling. I'm setting up an editor stub that does nothing so I can simulate the empty-message case and see what git actually does.

For the `-m` case running through prepare-commit-msg, since the hook isn't attached to a TTY in the scratch repo, CanPromptInteractively should be false, so it auto-links without prompting — that's the expected, correct behavior. Now let me write the overlay test to cover these cases.

content.text:
Here's the pre-edit brief for the commit-msg fix. Nothing is edited. I reproduced the gap with real `git commit` and Entire's installed hooks, and it's wider than the comment character.

## Problem

The commit-msg hook (`CommitMsg`) removes Entire's trailer when the message has no user content, so git still aborts an empty commit. It judges "content" wrong in three cases. Real git results, the same on main (`f36367e6f`) and the PR head (`866efab31`):

| Case | Should | Actually |
| --- | --- | --- |
| editor, `#` (default), nothing typed | abort | aborts ✓ |
| editor, `core.commentChar=;`, nothing typed | abort | commits. On main the message is the trailer plus Entire's `#` helper lines; on `866efab31` it's the trailer only. |
| editor with `-v` / `commit.verbose`, `#`, nothing typed | abort | commits a message holding only `Entire-Checkpoint: …` |
| `git commit -m "#42 fix login"` | keep the trailer | trailer removed, so the commit loses its checkpoint link |

## Root cause

`hasUserContent` ([manual_commit_hooks.go:300](cmd/entire/cli/strategy/manual_commit_hooks.go:300)) treats exactly `#` lines as comments, everywhere in the message. Git's cleanup works differently in two ways:
- In an editor message, git drops lines starting with the configured prefix, plus everything from the scissors line down. So `;` lines and the `-v` diff got counted as user content.
- In a `-m`/`-F` message, git keeps every line. So `#42 fix login` was wrongly treated as a comment.

The hook isn't told which kind of message it has, but the message shows it: an editor message ends with git's comment block (above any scissors line), while a `-m`/`-F` message ends with its own text, and after prepare that's Entire's trailer.

## Two options

- **A, prefix only (your ask as stated):** use `gitCommentPrefix` in `hasUserContent` and stop at the exact scissors line. This fixes the `;` and `-v` rows but leaves the `-m "#42"` link loss.
- **B, my pick:** A, plus treat prefix lines as comments only when the message actually ends with git's comment block. This fixes all three rows, in the same function, for about 5 more lines.
  - One edge gets worse: a user who deletes git's comment block, deletes Entire's helper lines, and types only `#`-prefixed lines would commit a trailer-only message instead of aborting. I'll note it in a code comment.
  - Perf: if the message ends with an `Entire-Checkpoint:` line (the agent `-m` path), every line is content and no `git config` call is needed. Editor commits pay one call (about 5 ms).

## Proposed change (B), one commit on this branch

- `CommitMsg` resolves the prefix only when it's needed, then calls `hasUserContent(message, commentPrefix)`.
- `hasUserContent` cuts at the exact scissors line. When the remaining text ends with a prefix line, it drops prefix lines. When it doesn't, it keeps every line. Either way it ignores `Entire-Checkpoint:` lines and blanks.
- `stripCheckpointTrailer` stays as is.

## Tests, written first and checked to fail

- **Integration** (real hook binaries, in `checkpoint_trailer_authority_test.go`):
  - an untouched editor message with `;`, and with `#` plus a `-v` scissors line and diff: prepare, then commit-msg, must leave no checkpoint trailer, so git aborts;
  - `-m "#42 fix login"`: commit-msg must keep the trailer;
  - plain `#` stays as a guard.

  Of these, only the guard passes today.
- **Unit table for `hasUserContent`:**
  - only comments under `#`, `;` and `//`;
  - `-v` diff below the scissors line;
  - a typed line;
  - `-m "#42"` with a trailer;
  - an empty `-m` with a trailer;
  - an editor message whose git block was deleted but Entire's helper lines kept.
- **Reverse check:** after the fix, put the old behaviors back one at a time in scratch copies and confirm the tests catch each one.

## Verification

- `mise run fmt && mise run lint`.
- Strategy, cli and integration packages with `-race`.
- `mise run test:e2e:canary`.
- The four real-`git commit` cases above, rerun against the new binary.
- Then a local commit. No push until you approve, and I'll draft the PR description addition for approval at that point.

input.content:
fix(strategy): judge an empty commit message the way git's cleanup will

The commit-msg hook removes Entire's trailer when the user left the
message empty, so git still aborts the commit. It counted exactly the
"#" lines as comments, everywhere in the message, which git's cleanup
does not do:

- an editor message with core.commentChar=";" (or any other prefix), or
  a `commit -v` message with its diff below the scissors line, counted
  as having content, so git recorded a commit holding only the trailer
  instead of aborting;
- a `-m "#42 fix login"` message counted as empty, so the hook removed
  the trailer and the commit lost its checkpoint link.

git does not tell commit-msg how the message was written, but the
message shows it: an editor message ends with git's comment block, a
-m/-F message ends with its own text (after prepare, the trailer).
Prefix lines now count as comments only when that block ends the
message, using git's comment prefix and cutting at the exact scissors
line. A message that ends with its trailer skips the git config lookup.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

content.text:
Committed locally as `4cfd66130`, on top of `866efab31`. The branch is 1 ahead of origin and merges cleanly with main (`f36367e6f`). Nothing has been pushed.

**What it does:**
- Lines starting with the comment prefix now count as comments only when git's comment block ends the message.
- The check uses the repository's comment prefix and stops at the exact scissors line.
- A message that ends with its trailer (the agent `-m` path) skips the `git config` lookup entirely.

**Verification:**
- **Tests that failed before the fix:** the `;` and `-v` untouched-editor integration tests and the `-m "#42"` test. The default-`#` guard passed throughout.
- **Reverse check:** putting each old behavior back made the new tests fail, all 4 times.
- **Real `git commit` with all three hooks installed:**
  - nothing typed under `#`, `;` or `-v`: git aborts;
  - `-m "#42 fix login"`: keeps its trailer;
  - a typed subject under `#`, `;`, `auto` and `-v`: commits with the trailer and a clean message.
- **Lint:** 0 issues.
- **Packages:** with `-race`, `cli`, `trailers` and integration are ok. `strategy`'s only failures are the `TestInstallHooks_*` timeouts described above.
- **Canary:** Vogon 53/53, Roger-Roger 4/4.

**PR description addition, for approval:**

1. In **Fix**, add after the "Prepare reads the message…" paragraph:
   > The commit-msg hook's empty-message check now counts content the way git's cleanup will. git does not tell commit-msg how the message was written, but an editor message ends with git's comment block and a `-m`/`-F` message ends with its own text, so prefix lines count as comments only when that block ends the message, using the same comment prefix and exact scissors line. Before, an untouched editor message with `core.commentChar=;` or `commit -v` was committed holding only the trailer instead of aborting, and `git commit -m "#42 fix login"` lost its trailer; both also happen on main.
2. In **Tests, verified RED before the fix**, add:
   > - `TestTrailerAuthority_UntouchedEditorMessageAborts` (`;` and `commit -v`) failed with `commit-msg must remove the trailer so git aborts the empty commit`, and `TestTrailerAuthority_MessageSubjectStartingWithHashKeepsTrailer` with `commit-msg must keep the trailer of a message with content`. Its default-prefix case is a guard.
3. In **Test plan**, replace the real-`git commit` line with:
   > - [x] real `git commit` with `core.commentChar` unset, `;`, `//` and `auto`, fresh and amend; with the commit-msg hook installed, an untouched editor message aborts under `#`, `;` and `commit -v`, and `-m "#42 fix login"` keeps its trailer
